fields.Front:
You manage a 12-person marketing team adopting an AI assistant. Last year the team's vendor updated its models three times, and each update made parts of the team's shared "best prompts" document obsolete. You are planning this year's AI training investment.

Which approach best reflects the rationale for AI Fluency given in Anthropic's AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations course?

A. Fund training on the current model's best prompts, settings, and features, and repeat it after each vendor update.
B. Train everyone in prompt-writing principles that carry across models, and leave the review of outputs to the team's two editors.
C. Train two power users in each new model's quirks, shortcuts, and limits, and route the rest of the team's AI requests through them.
D. Train everyone in lasting skills for deciding what to delegate, communicating intent, evaluating outputs, and acting responsibly.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D matches the course's core premise: AI Fluency is a lasting framework of competencies (the 4Ds of Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence) that stays relevant as AI technology evolves, unlike temporary tips and tricks. Option A is the tactical, tool-specific training the course says can quickly become outdated, so each model update would send the team back to the same retraining. Option B invests in a transferable skill but in only one of them: it trains Description for everyone and hands evaluation to two editors, while the course's lasting framework is all four competencies together, Discernment and Diligence included. Option C concentrates fragile model-specific knowledge in two people instead of building transferable skills across the team. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) References: • Introduction to AI Fluency — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • The 4D Framework — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Framework for AI Fluency, v1.1 (Dakan & Feller, Ringling College)

fields.Front:
You lead communications at a nonprofit. You configure an AI assistant with your organization's background, voice guidelines, and standard response procedures so it can handle routine donor inquiries on the team's behalf, rather than giving it one task at a time.

In the AI Fluency Framework, which way of engaging with AI does this arrangement represent?

A. Automation
B. Augmentation
C. Agency
D. Delegation
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: Agency means configuring AI to work independently on your behalf, establishing its knowledge and behavior patterns rather than issuing specific task instructions, which is exactly what this setup describes. Option A, Automation, is the AI completing specific tasks based on your direct instructions, the pattern this arrangement moves beyond. Option B, Augmentation, is back-and-forth collaboration in which you and the AI work as thinking and task-execution partners. Option D, Delegation, is not one of the three ways of engaging at all; it is one of the 4D competencies, the skill of deciding what work to do with AI versus yourself. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) References: • Why do we need AI Fluency? (AI Fluency course) • The 4D Framework — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Framework for AI Fluency, v1.1 (Dakan & Feller, Ringling College)

fields.Front:
You are a student who plans carefully which parts of each assignment to work on with an AI assistant, double-checks every fact in its drafts, and acknowledges its role as your program's policy requires. Yet your last four sessions began with one-line requests like "help with my sociology paper," and each first draft missed your topic and needed extensive rework.

Which AI Fluency competency most needs development?

A. Delegation
B. Description
C. Discernment
D. Diligence
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Description is the competency of communicating clearly with AI, defining what you want, how the AI should approach it, and how it should interact with you. Vague one-line requests are precisely that gap, and Anthropic's AI Fluency course stresses that AI cannot read your mind. Option A is already handled, since you thoughtfully decide which parts of each assignment to work on with AI. Option C is also in place, because every fact gets double-checked. Option D is covered by the required acknowledgment; the weak first drafts stem from thin communication, not from irresponsible use. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) References: • The 4D Framework — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • A closer look at Description (AI Fluency course) • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct

fields.Front:
You are rolling AI out to your consulting team. Anthropic's AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations course defines AI Fluency as working effectively, efficiently, ethically, and safely. Your rollout plan so far is built around getting strong results from the assistant quickly, and it is silent on how client data is protected, whether clients are told AI was involved, and who answers for errors in client deliverables.

Which competency does the course say addresses the ethical and safety goals in that definition?

A. Diligence
B. Discernment
C. Delegation
D. Description
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: the course states that while Delegation, Description, and Discernment focus primarily on effectiveness and efficiency, Diligence addresses the ethical and safety aspects of AI collaboration, covering responsibility, transparency, and accountability. The plan's three gaps map onto its three parts: how client data is protected is Creation Diligence, whether clients are told AI was involved is Transparency Diligence, and who answers for errors is Deployment Diligence. Option B, Discernment, is the critical evaluation of outputs, processes, and behavior, which the course groups with the effectiveness-oriented competencies. Option C, Delegation, concerns deciding how to divide work between you and AI. Option D, Description, concerns communicating your intent clearly; neither of those two addresses the ethical and safety goals directly. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) References: • A closer look at Diligence — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • The Description-Discernment loop — What's next (AI Fluency course) • The 4D Framework — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You manage a team rolling out an AI assistant. A colleague argues to you that the AI Fluency Framework's 4D competencies only matter for interactive chat sessions, and that configuring an assistant to act independently on the team's behalf calls for an entirely different skill set.

Which response best reflects the position taken in Anthropic's AI Fluency course?

A. Each competency maps to one way of engaging: Delegation governs Automation, Description governs Augmentation, and Discernment governs Agency.
B. The same four competencies apply across Automation, Augmentation, and Agency, including configuring AI to act on your behalf.
C. The 4Ds cover Automation and Augmentation, but Agency requires a separate technical framework.
D. The 4Ds are a transitional skill set that will be replaced as models become more capable.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B states the course's position directly: the four competencies apply across all three ways of engaging with AI, and shaping an assistant's knowledge and behavior for independent work draws on the same Delegation, Description, Discernment, and Diligence skills. Option A invents a one-to-one mapping between competencies and engagement modes that the course never makes. Option C carves Agency out of the framework, while the course presents the 4Ds as spanning it. Option D contradicts the course's claim that the framework is designed to remain relevant as AI capabilities evolve. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) References: • The 4D Framework — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Conclusion (AI Fluency course) • Framework for AI Fluency, v1.1 (Dakan & Feller, Ringling College)

fields.Front:
You are an analyst who runs the identical summarization prompt on the same 10-page briefing twice in separate sessions. Both summaries are accurate and cover every section of the briefing, but their wording, ordering, and emphasis differ noticeably, and a teammate concludes the tool is malfunctioning.

What best explains the differing outputs?

A. The assistant looks up stored summaries, so each session can return a different stored match for the briefing.
B. The briefing overflows the model's context window, so each session reads a different portion of the text.
C. The model generates text probabilistically, so the same prompt yields different, equally valid summaries.
D. The software is deterministic, so one of the sessions must have received a different prompt or file.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: generative AI creates new content through probabilistic generation rather than retrieving stored answers, so variation between runs of the same prompt is expected behavior, not a malfunction. Option A describes a database-lookup model of AI that the AI Fluency course explicitly contrasts with generative systems, which write new text instead of returning stored text. Option B does not fit, because a 10-page briefing is far smaller than a current model's context window, and an input that did not fit would not yield two summaries that each cover every section. Option D carries over the logic of traditional software, which returns identical output for identical input; the course describes language models as non-deterministic by default, and the scenario says the prompt and the briefing were identical. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • Glossary — Temperature • Capabilities & limitations (AI Fluency course) • Generative AI fundamentals (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You are a student explaining to your study group how the AI assistant that drafts text differs from the spam filter on the university's mail system, which sorts each incoming message into legitimate mail or junk.

Which distinction matches the definition of generative AI given in Anthropic's AI Fluency course?

A. Generative AI creates new content, while systems like the spam filter analyze and classify content that already exists.
B. Generative AI follows hand-written rules, while the spam filter learns statistical patterns from data.
C. Generative AI looks up its responses in a curated database of pre-written documents.
D. Generative AI must be retrained for each new kind of task, while the spam filter switches tasks without retraining.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A captures the course's definition: generative AI is distinguished by its ability to create new content such as text, images, and code, rather than only analyzing or classifying existing data, which is what the spam filter does. Option B misdescribes generative AI, since modern generative models learn patterns from vast training data rather than following hand-written rules. Option C describes retrieval, not generation; the course emphasizes that these systems generate rather than look up. Option D inverts a course point: generative models can switch between diverse tasks without additional training. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • Generative AI fundamentals (AI Fluency course) • Capabilities & limitations — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Glossary — LLM

fields.Front:
You manage a customer-insights team. A teammate asks how your AI assistant can both discuss an obscure historical topic in depth and reliably follow instructions like "give me three bullet points in a formal tone."

Which explanation matches the two-stage learning process described in Anthropic's AI Fluency course?

A. Fine-tuning builds broad knowledge of the world from vast amounts of text, and pre-training then teaches the model to follow instructions.
B. The model memorizes a fact database during training and consults a built-in search engine whenever it needs to follow instructions.
C. The model learns continuously during each conversation, permanently updating its training as it reads your messages and replies.
D. Pre-training builds broad capability from patterns in vast amounts of text, and fine-tuning then teaches the model to follow instructions.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D matches the course: generative AI learns first through pre-training, absorbing patterns from vast amounts of text, and then through fine-tuning, in which it learns to follow instructions and provide helpful responses. Option A names the right stages but swaps their roles. Option B substitutes a database-plus-search picture that the course contrasts with how generative models actually work. Option C confuses conversation with training; reading your messages provides temporary context within a session but does not update the model's underlying training. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • Capabilities & limitations — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Glossary — Pretraining • Glossary — Fine-tuning

fields.Front:
You are an analyst who has just learned that your AI assistant generates responses probabilistically rather than retrieving stored answers, and that it can produce confident, fluent text that is wrong.

Which adjustment to your working style follows most directly from that understanding?

A. Run each question three times in separate chats and rely on the claims that appear in each of the three replies.
B. Treat first responses as drafts to refine through iteration, and verify factual claims before relying on them.
C. Invest in one detailed prompt covering the full set of requirements, and treat the first reply as final.
D. Spot-check the passages where the assistant sounds unsure, and trust the passages that read as fluent and confident.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B draws the right working implications: because outputs are generated rather than retrieved, results vary and improve through iterative refinement, and because generation can be confidently wrong, factual claims need verification. Anthropic's AI Fluency course frames AI as an interactive partner, not a database or vending machine. Option A mistakes agreement for accuracy: a model can reproduce the same inaccuracy run after run, so matching replies do not verify a claim. Option C relies on Description alone: a detailed prompt improves the odds of a good first reply but cannot rule out confident errors, and treating the first reply as final skips both iteration and checking. Option D treats fluency and confidence as evidence of accuracy, exactly the trap hallucinations exploit, because a wrong claim can read as smoothly as a right one. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • Capabilities & limitations (AI Fluency course) • A closer look at Description — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Reduce hallucinations

fields.Front:
You lead communications at a nonprofit. In March you ask an AI assistant that has no web search or other live-data tools, with no documents attached, to list foundation grant deadlines for this spring's cycle, which the funders announced in February. It fluently lists five programs with dates, but when you check, three of the deadlines are from a previous year's cycle.

Which limitation most directly explains the unreliable list?

A. The model's training data ends at a cutoff date, so it cannot know this cycle's deadlines.
B. The request exceeded the model's context window, so part of your question was dropped before it answered.
C. The prompt failed to define a role and tone for the assistant, so it answered as a generalist.
D. The model's wording was too confident; instructing it to hedge would have made the dates accurate.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A identifies the root limitation: models have knowledge cutoff dates, so recent and currently changing facts like this cycle's deadlines lie beyond their training data, and with no web search and no documents to draw on, the model instead produces plausible dates from older patterns. Option B does not fit, because a short question is nowhere near context limits and nothing was dropped. Option C is a style consideration that cannot supply information the model does not have. Option D confuses presentation with substance: hedged wording changes the tone of the claims, not the model's access to current facts; the fix is supplying current information yourself, giving the assistant a tool such as web search, or verifying against live sources. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • How up-to-date is Claude's training data? (Claude Help Center) • Capabilities & limitations — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Enable and use web search (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
You are a student who asks an AI assistant for sources on a psychology topic. It returns five citations with authors, journals, years, and page numbers in flawless format. Checking the library database, you find two of the cited papers do not exist.

What does this behavior illustrate?

A. Context window overflow: the session ran out of room, so real citations were cut down into incomplete fragments.
B. A knowledge cutoff: the two papers were published after the model's training data ended, so it could not know them.
C. Hallucination: the model can generate plausible, confidently formatted content that is factually false.
D. Deliberate deception: the model detects academic queries and intentionally fabricates sources to appear helpful.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C names the limitation that Anthropic's AI Fluency course highlights: hallucination is factually incorrect output, and fabricated citations are a classic case. Polished formatting and confident presentation are no evidence of existence, so sources must be independently verified before use. Option A is wrong because the fake citations are complete and well formed, not truncated fragments. Option B cannot explain sources that never existed at all; a cutoff hides real recent work, it does not create fictional papers. Option D attributes intent the mechanism does not have, since hallucination is a byproduct of probabilistic generation, not detection and deceit. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • Reduce hallucinations • Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What's going on? (Claude Help Center) • Capabilities & limitations — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You are an analyst in a single long working session with an AI assistant over a 200-page report. Early on, its answers about chapter details are consistently accurate. Two hours and many exchanges later, it starts contradicting specifics that were established near the beginning of the conversation.

Which limitation best explains the change?

A. Hallucination: the model fills gaps in a dense report with plausible but invented details, so answers can contain fabricated specifics.
B. The context window: the model holds a finite amount of text, so in a long session the earliest details are dropped or condensed.
C. The knowledge cutoff: the report's subject postdates the model's training data, so the model cannot recall its details.
D. Non-deterministic generation: the model samples its output probabilistically, so each reply can differ from the last.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: a context window bounds how much conversation and document text the model can consider at once. As a very long session fills it, the earliest material is dropped first or condensed into summaries, and recall of what remains becomes less reliable, which produces contradictions of previously established facts. Option A names a real limitation, but hallucination describes plausible-sounding incorrect statements in general; it does not explain why answers that were consistently accurate early on degraded only after a long session. Option C fails because the report was supplied directly in the session and early answers were accurate, so training data is not the constraint. Option D names a real property, run-to-run variation, but it offers no reason for answers that stayed accurate for two hours to begin contradicting details from the start of the conversation. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.1 References: • Context windows — How the context window works • How large is the context window on paid Claude plans? — Automatic context management (Claude Help Center) • Capabilities & limitations — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You are an analyst producing a market report with an AI assistant. You are concerned specifically about two limitations that Anthropic's AI Fluency course highlights: hallucination and the model's knowledge cutoff.

Which TWO practices most directly mitigate those limitations? (Select TWO.)

A. Ask the assistant to rate its confidence in each claim and publish those rated above 90 percent as they stand.
B. Verify specific factual claims, statistics, and citations against independent sources before publishing.
C. Rerun the same prompt three times and publish the figures that appear in each of the three runs.
D. Supply the latest market figures in your prompt instead of relying on the model's built-in knowledge of recent data.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B and D. Option B directly counters hallucination: because models can generate plausible but false specifics, independent verification before publication is the reliable control. Option D directly counters the knowledge cutoff: providing current figures in the prompt gives the model information its training data cannot contain. Option A leans on self-reported confidence, which is not a dependable signal of factual accuracy, so a confidently wrong claim would be published as it stands. Option C mistakes consistency for correctness: comparing runs can expose inconsistencies that hint at a hallucination, but a model can reproduce the same inaccuracy in every run, and agreement between runs does nothing about data newer than the cutoff. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • Reduce hallucinations • How up-to-date is Claude's training data? (Claude Help Center) • Capabilities & limitations — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You manage a research team at a nonprofit that is finishing a report on a community health study carried out with three partner communities. You are sorting the remaining tasks between the team and an AI assistant, applying the view in Anthropic's AI Fluency course that the most effective applications leverage the complementary strengths of humans and AI.

Which task is the strongest candidate to keep primarily with people?

A. Translating the executive summary into Spanish for a bilingual colleague to review.
B. Producing first-pass summaries of published research articles for later review.
C. Brainstorming twenty candidate titles for the final report's public release.
D. Deciding whether to publish findings that put one of the partner communities at risk.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is the judgment call: weighing potential harm to a partner community is exactly the kind of ethical decision the course says humans must supply, since critical thinking, contextual judgment, and ethical oversight are the human half of the partnership. Option A is a language task, and translating between languages is among the strengths the course attributes to AI; a colleague's review stays in the loop. Option B suits AI well because human review is already planned downstream. Option C is low-stakes idea generation where breadth matters more than accountability; none of these three carries the ethical weight that makes Option D human-led. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • Capabilities & limitations — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • A closer look at Delegation — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You lead communications at a nonprofit and are eager to use AI for the annual appeal. You spend two hours prompting an assistant and collect 14 candidate letters, but you cannot choose among them because you never defined the campaign's goal, its audience, or what a successful appeal would accomplish.

In the AI Fluency Framework, which Delegation component was skipped?

A. Problem Awareness
B. Platform Awareness
C. Task Delegation
D. Performance Description
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: Problem Awareness means clearly understanding your goals and the nature of the work before involving AI, and the missing definition of goal, audience, and success is exactly why 14 drafts cannot be evaluated. Option B concerns knowing what different AI systems can and cannot do, which is not the bottleneck here. Option C, strategically dividing work between you and the AI, cannot be done sensibly until the goal itself is clear. Option D belongs to the Description competency and governs how the AI behaves during a collaboration, not whether you know what you are trying to achieve. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • A closer look at Delegation — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Define success criteria and build evaluations — Define your success criteria • Prompt engineering overview — Before prompt engineering

fields.Front:
You are an analyst who plans a competitive brief assuming your AI assistant can pull this morning's market prices and browse your company's internal sales database. Mid-project you discover it can do neither, and a full day of planned work has to be redone by hand. Your project goal itself was well defined from the start.

In the AI Fluency Framework, which Delegation component most needs development?

A. Task Delegation
B. Platform Awareness
C. Problem Awareness
D. Transparency Diligence
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Platform Awareness is understanding the capabilities and limitations of different AI systems, and the wasted day came from assuming access to live prices and internal databases that this assistant does not have. Option A is downstream, because task splits built on mistaken capability assumptions fail no matter how thoughtfully the work is divided. Option C is explicitly satisfied in the scenario, since the goal was well defined. Option D concerns being open about AI's role in your finished work, which has nothing to do with misjudging what the system can do. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • A closer look at Delegation — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Capabilities & limitations (AI Fluency course) • Framework for AI Fluency, v1.1 (Dakan & Feller, Ringling College)

fields.Front:
You are a student assembling a capstone presentation with an AI assistant. Four tasks remain: choosing the central argument, confirming that quoted passages match the original source documents on your desk, reformatting speaker notes across 30 slides into one consistent bullet style, and making the final call on which counterarguments to address.

Which task is the strongest candidate to hand off largely to the assistant?

A. Choosing the central argument
B. Confirming the quoted passages match the sources
C. Reformatting the speaker notes across the 30 slides
D. Making the final call on which counterarguments to address
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C fits Task Delegation in the AI Fluency Framework best: consistent reformatting across 30 slides is well specified, mechanical, and plays to AI speed and versatility, with results that are easy for you to spot-check. Option A is the intellectual core of the work, where your own expertise and point of view must lead. Option B requires checking text against physical source documents the assistant cannot see, and accuracy verification is exactly where the AI Fluency course says human oversight belongs. Option D is a judgment call about your audience and argument strategy, the kind of decision the course says to keep with the human partner. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • A closer look at Delegation — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Project planning and Delegation — Step 3: Task breakdown and delegation analysis (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You manage a nine-person research team and are writing delegation guidance for AI-assisted projects. You want the guidance to follow the approach to Task Delegation taught in Anthropic's AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations course.

Which TWO practices reflect that approach? (Select TWO.)

A. Break each project into tasks and decide for each whether you, the AI, or a collaboration between you fits it best.
B. Give the assistant the tasks it can finish faster than a person would, and keep the remaining tasks with the team.
C. Keep tasks that hinge on human judgment, domain expertise, or ethical weight with people.
D. Hand each project to the assistant in full at first, and take back individual tasks when it visibly struggles.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and C. Option A is the mechanics of Task Delegation as the course teaches it: thoughtful, per-task decisions about what to do yourself, what to do together with AI, and what to let AI handle. Option C applies the guiding principle that delegation should leverage the complementary strengths of each partner, keeping judgment-heavy and ethically weighty work with humans. Option B uses speed as its only test, which would hand judgment-heavy tasks to the assistant whenever it is faster; the course says the goal is not to automate everything but to create the most effective human-AI partnership. Option D inverts thoughtful delegation into delegation by default: the course asks you to define your goals and understand the work before bringing AI in, not to discover misfits through visible failures. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • A closer look at Delegation — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • A closer look at Delegation — Exercises (AI Fluency course) • Project planning and Delegation — Step 3: Task breakdown and delegation analysis (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You are a manager planning a conference-workshop project you will run with an AI assistant over the next month, and you want to follow the project-planning approach taught in Anthropic's AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations course.

Which sequence matches that approach?

A. Ask the assistant to generate the complete deliverable immediately, then define goals and plan around whatever gaps appear.
B. Choose your AI tools first, list what each one does well, then look for project tasks that match those strengths.
C. Break the project into major tasks, delegate all of them to the assistant, and keep only final proofreading for yourself.
D. Define the vision and what success looks like, break the work into major tasks, then make a delegation decision for each.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D mirrors the course's project exercise: establish a clear vision of what success looks like first, identify the major tasks, and then analyze each task for whether it needs human strengths, AI capabilities, or collaboration. Option A postpones both vision and planning until after generation, leaving you to reverse-engineer goals from an unguided output. Option B lets tools drive the work, the opposite of starting from Problem Awareness. Option C is wholesale handoff rather than delegation, ignoring the per-task analysis and keeping human judgment out of everything but proofreading. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • Project planning and Delegation — Step 2: Project vision and goals (AI Fluency course) • A closer look at Delegation — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Define success criteria and build evaluations — Define your success criteria

fields.Front:
You are an analyst asked to assess regulatory filings in an industry you know nothing about. You propose delegating the analysis entirely to an AI assistant, reasoning that it knows far more about this domain than you do.

What key risk does the treatment of Delegation in Anthropic's AI Fluency course highlight in this plan?

A. The assistant will refuse tasks that fall outside your own documented area of expertise.
B. Without domain expertise, you cannot judge what to delegate or whether the output is sound.
C. The only real risk is under-specification: sufficiently detailed prompts make delegating unfamiliar work safe.
D. The main risk is efficiency, because models work more slowly on dense regulatory text.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B states the course's point: effective delegation requires both an understanding of AI capabilities and your own domain expertise, because expertise is what lets you divide the work sensibly and discern whether results are trustworthy. Delegating precisely because you cannot evaluate the work removes the human check. Option A invents a refusal behavior that is not the issue. Option C treats prompt detail as a substitute for expertise, but detailed instructions cannot come from, or be judged by, someone who cannot assess the subject. Option D reframes a judgment-and-oversight problem as a speed problem. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • A closer look at Delegation — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Conclusion — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • A closer look at Discernment — Exercises (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You are an analyst who prompts an assistant with "write something about our Q3 results." You receive fluent generic prose, but what you actually wanted was a one-page memo for the executive team, in bullet form, highlighting three specific risks.

In the AI Fluency Framework, which Description component was missing from your prompt?

A. Product Description
B. Process Description
C. Performance Description
D. Platform Awareness
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: Product Description means clearly defining what you want in terms of outputs, format, audience, and style, and none of the one-page memo, bullet format, executive audience, or three specific risks made it into the prompt. Option B governs how the assistant should approach the work, such as its method or sequence of steps, which is not what went wrong here. Option C governs how the assistant behaves during the collaboration, such as being concise or challenging. Option D is not a Description component at all; it belongs to Delegation and concerns knowing what AI systems can do. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • A closer look at Description — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct • Introduction to prompt design (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
You are a student who asks an assistant for feedback on an essay. You wanted it to first check your argument's structure against the assignment rubric and only then comment on style, but instead it rewrites the whole essay in its own voice.

Using the AI Fluency Framework's three types of Description, what is the most effective addition to your next prompt?

A. A Product Description asking for a longer, more detailed response that covers each section of the essay.
B. A Process Description asking the assistant to check the argument against the rubric first, then comment on style, without rewriting.
C. A Performance Description asking the assistant to be more encouraging and supportive in how it delivers feedback.
D. A Process Description asking the assistant to comment on style first, then check the argument against the rubric, without rewriting.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B addresses the actual failure: Process Description guides how the AI approaches your request, and specifying the sequence of rubric-based evaluation first, then style comments, with rewriting explicitly off the table, directs the method you wanted. Option A is a Product Description, which defines what the output should be; asking for a longer, more detailed response changes the amount of output rather than the approach, and length was never the problem. Option C is a Performance Description, which shapes how the AI behaves with you, such as being more encouraging; adjusting tone does not stop wholesale rewriting. Option D is also a Process Description, but it reverses the sequence you asked for, putting style comments ahead of the rubric check, so it does not direct the method you wanted. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • A closer look at Description — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct

fields.Front:
You are a manager using an AI assistant as a thinking partner on a reorganization plan. Its analyses are competent, but it agrees with every idea you float, and its long answers bury the key points. You want it to challenge your assumptions and keep responses brief.

In the AI Fluency Framework, which Description component addresses what you want to change?

A. Product Description
B. Process Description
C. Performance Description
D. Task Delegation
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: Performance Description defines how you want the AI to behave during the collaboration, and the AI Fluency course names exactly the dimensions at issue, challenging versus supportive and concise versus detailed. Option A defines the artifact you want produced, but your complaint is about interaction style, not a deliverable. Option B guides the method the assistant uses to work through a task, not its collaborative demeanor. Option D is a Delegation component about dividing work between you and the AI, which is not in question here. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • A closer look at Description — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • The AI Fluency Index — Developing your own AI fluency (Anthropic Education Report)

fields.Front:
You lead donor communications and are nine revision rounds into a fundraising letter with an AI assistant. Each round you reply only "not quite right, try again," and each new draft misses in a new way.

What change would most improve the collaboration?

A. Keep replying "try again" for a few more rounds, since random variation between drafts will eventually match your vision.
B. Switch to a larger, more capable model that can infer the intent behind the same one-line feedback you have been giving.
C. Ask the assistant to attach a confidence score to each new draft, and keep working only from the high-confidence drafts.
D. State the letter's audience, tone, key points, and format up front, then say specifically what to change each round.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D applies the core principle of Description in the AI Fluency Framework: AI cannot read your mind, and the quality of results comes down to how clearly you articulate what you want and give feedback the assistant can act on. The nine wasted rounds trace to content-free feedback, not model quality. Option A is the vending-machine approach the AI Fluency course warns against, paying for missing clarity with rounds of luck. Option B upgrades the model to compensate for missing communication, but no model can reliably infer requirements you never stated. Option C adds self-reported confidence, which measures nothing about fit with preferences the assistant was never told. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct • A closer look at Description — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
You run communications for a nonprofit with a distinctive voice in its social posts. Prompts describing the voice in adjectives, like "warm but not saccharine, direct but hopeful," keep producing drafts that miss it.

Which prompting technique from Anthropic's AI Fluency course most directly targets this problem?

A. Ask the assistant to think through the voice guidelines step by step before drafting each post.
B. Break the drafting into a sequence of smaller steps: headline first, then body text, then hashtags.
C. Include several past posts that capture the voice and ask for new posts in the same style.
D. Specify a strict word-count constraint and a fixed structure for every post.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is the course's show-examples technique, and it fits precisely: style and voice are easier to demonstrate than to describe, so past posts that embody the voice give the model a concrete target that adjectives have failed to convey. Option A helps with reasoning-heavy tasks, but the problem here is stylistic calibration, not reasoning. Option B decomposes complexity, and drafting a short post is not a multi-step problem. Option D constrains length and structure, which does nothing to communicate voice. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.2 References: • Prompting best practices — Use examples effectively • Effective prompting techniques — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Prompt engineering best practices for 2026 — How to use prompt engineering (claude.com)

fields.Front:
You are an analyst whose single prompt asks an assistant to extract figures from a spreadsheet summary, compute quarterly trends, compare two competitors, draft an executive summary, and recommend actions, all at once. Responses are shallow, and the trend computation is routinely skipped.

Which prompting technique most directly addresses this?

A. Define a role for the assistant, such as "act as a senior financial analyst," at the top of the prompt.
B. Break the task into separate prompts for extraction, analysis, comparison, and drafting, run in that order.
C. Add emphasis words such as "thorough," "detailed," and "comprehensive" to the task description.
D. Include one example of a finished executive summary in the prompt as a model for the output.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is the technique Anthropic's AI Fluency course teaches for exactly this failure: breaking complex work into steps guides the model through multi-step reasoning, ensuring each stage, including the skipped trend computation, gets attention before the next begins. Option A shifts persona and tone but leaves five competing tasks crammed into one pass. Option C adds vague emphasis without restructuring the work, so the steps still compete for attention. Option D shows what the end product looks like while leaving the intermediate analysis unguided, so the summary may read better while still resting on skipped computation. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • Effective prompting techniques — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Prompting best practices — Chain complex prompts • My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
You are an analyst whose prompt for a complex data summary, written for an AI assistant, keeps producing off-target results after several rewrites, and you are not sure how to improve it.

Which tactic does Anthropic's AI Fluency course recommend as its "secret weapon" here?

A. Ask the assistant to critique your prompt, pointing out what is ambiguous and what context it still needs.
B. Open a fresh conversation, paste in the same prompt verbatim, and compare the new result with the old.
C. Conclude the model is faulty and move the task to a different platform with a stronger model.
D. Cut the prompt down to its core request, removing the background detail and examples.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is the course's secret weapon: asking the AI to help improve your prompt turns the collaboration onto the communication problem itself, surfacing ambiguities and missing context you cannot see from inside your own framing. Option B changes nothing about the prompt, so it reruns the same failure from a clean slate. Option C blames the platform before fixing the communication, and the same unclear prompt travels with you. Option D strips out background detail and examples, which can delete exactly the context the model lacks, since the issue is missing and ambiguous information, not prompt length. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.2 References: • Effective prompting techniques — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Prompt engineering overview — Before prompt engineering

fields.Front:
You are a student preparing for a policy debate. Plain requests for practice questions yield friendly, softball quizzing, but you want realistic practice against pointed opposition in a formal debate register.

Which prompting technique most directly gets you what you want?

A. Specify a constraint limiting each practice question and answer to a fixed length.
B. Show the assistant examples of the friendly questions it asked previously so it can build on them.
C. Ask the assistant to think through each question step by step before posing it to you.
D. Tell the assistant to act as a skeptical opposing debater who challenges you in a formal register.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D applies the technique of defining the AI's role or tone from Anthropic's AI Fluency course, which is exactly the lever for changing how the assistant engages: a skeptical-opponent role in a formal register produces the adversarial practice the plain requests never asked for. Option A controls length, not stance. Option B feeds back examples of the friendly behavior you want to move away from, anchoring it further. Option C deepens the quality of individual questions but leaves the collegial framing untouched. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.2 References: • Effective prompting techniques — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Prompting best practices — Give Claude a role

fields.Front:
You are an analyst reviewing an assistant's market analysis. Every figure checks out against your sources, but reading the reasoning, you find it compared one company's year-over-year growth with another's quarter-over-quarter growth without flagging the mismatch.

In the AI Fluency Framework, which type of Discernment caught this problem?

A. Product Discernment
B. Process Discernment
C. Performance Discernment
D. Deployment Diligence
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Process Discernment assesses how the AI arrived at its output, looking for logical errors, attention gaps, and inappropriate reasoning, and an apples-to-oranges comparison buried in otherwise accurate work is precisely a reasoning flaw rather than a factual one. Option A evaluates the quality of the output's content itself, and on that front every figure checked out. Option C evaluates the assistant's behavior within the collaboration, such as communication style and responsiveness. Option D is a Diligence component about taking responsibility for outputs you share, not a category of evaluation. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • A closer look at Discernment — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Reduce hallucinations — Advanced techniques

fields.Front:
You are a manager whose assistant produces reports with solid content, but during your working sessions it buries direct answers in long preambles, and it keeps ignoring your stated preference for bullet-point summaries.

In the AI Fluency Framework, which type of Discernment are you exercising when you evaluate this aspect of the collaboration?

A. Product Discernment
B. Process Discernment
C. Performance Discernment
D. Creation Diligence
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: Performance Discernment evaluates how the AI behaves within the collaboration itself, considering whether its communication style, responsiveness, and attention to your stated preferences serve your needs, which is exactly what burying answers and ignoring format preferences concern. Option A would apply to the reports' content, which you find solid. Option B would examine the reasoning behind an output rather than the interaction experience. Option D is a Diligence component about choosing AI systems thoughtfully and deciding what to share with them, not about evaluating collaborative behavior. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • A closer look at Discernment — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • A closer look at Discernment — Exercises (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You manage a consulting team and are writing review guidance for AI-drafted client briefs, which Anthropic's AI Fluency course warns can contain subtle, plausible-sounding errors.

Which TWO practices best reflect the course's approach to Discernment? (Select TWO.)

A. Give the closest review to drafts with awkward phrasing or formatting slips, and pass polished drafts after a quick read.
B. Have the assistant rate its confidence in each brief, and reserve human review for the drafts it rates low.
C. Check each brief's factual claims against independent sources, however authoritative the draft sounds.
D. Evaluate the reasoning behind each conclusion, and look for logical gaps even when the final prose reads smoothly.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C and D. Option C is core Product Discernment: because models generate plausible falsehoods fluently, accuracy must be established against independent sources, not surface authority. Option D is Process Discernment: the course says to assess how the AI arrived at its output, catching logical gaps that a polished final read-through misses. Option A triages by polish, but fluency and formatting are qualities of generation, not evidence of truth, so the smoothest drafts can still hold the subtle errors the course warns about. Option B leans on self-reported confidence, which is not a dependable accuracy signal, and it sends high-confidence drafts out with no human review, exactly where plausible errors are hardest to spot. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • A closer look at Discernment — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • The AI Fluency Index — Developing your own AI fluency (Anthropic Education Report) • Reduce hallucinations

fields.Front:
You manage a team that used an AI assistant to draft a 30-page technical white paper. Two colleagues volunteer to review it: a meticulous copyeditor with no background in the subject, and a subject-matter expert with modest editing skills. Anthropic's AI Fluency course notes that AI errors in such drafts tend to be plausible-sounding rather than obvious.

How should you assign the accuracy review?

A. Route it to the subject-matter expert, since domain knowledge is what lets a reviewer catch plausible-sounding errors.
B. Route it to the copyeditor alone, since grammar and consistency slips are the main risks in AI-drafted documents.
C. Skip human review and have the same assistant re-check its own draft for errors before the paper is released.
D. Give it to whichever volunteer is free first, since errors in AI drafts are typically easy for any careful reader to spot.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A follows the course's point that expertise powers Discernment: someone without domain knowledge struggles to judge the quality of plausible explanations, so accuracy review belongs with the subject-matter expert. Option B assigns the review to surface quality, but the stated risk is plausible falsehoods, which read as perfectly grammatical and consistent. Option C asks the system that produced the errors to certify itself, removing the independent human judgment Discernment requires. Option D rests on the assumption the scenario rules out, because these errors are plausible-sounding, not obvious to anyone. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • A closer look at Discernment — Exercises (AI Fluency course) • A closer look at Discernment — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What's going on? (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
You lead communications at a nonprofit. An assistant's draft of your impact report attributes a 38 percent increase in families served to your own 2024 annual report. Checking the annual report, you find no such statistic anywhere in it.

In the AI Fluency Framework, which type of Discernment did you exercise in catching this?

A. Process Discernment
B. Performance Discernment
C. Transparency Diligence
D. Product Discernment
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: Product Discernment evaluates the quality of the output itself, including accuracy, appropriateness, coherence, and relevance, and checking a claimed statistic against its cited source is a direct accuracy check on the product. Option A would examine the reasoning path the assistant took rather than the factual content of the draft. Option B concerns how the assistant behaves during the collaboration, such as its communication style and responsiveness. Option C is about being open regarding AI's role in your work, a disclosure question rather than an output-evaluation skill. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • A closer look at Discernment — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What's going on? (Claude Help Center) • Reduce hallucinations

fields.Front:
You are an analyst whose assistant returns a first draft that is largely on target, but the tone is too promotional and one section misunderstands your data. You are following the Description-Discernment loop from Anthropic's AI Fluency course.

What does the loop prescribe as your next move?

A. Discard the conversation and start from scratch with a brand-new prompt written from a blank page.
B. Accept the draft as final output and rework the promotional tone and the misread section yourself by hand.
C. Tell the assistant specifically what worked and what did not, then refine your description for another pass.
D. Resend the identical prompt until a better variant of the draft happens to appear on its own.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is the loop in action: after discerning the draft's specific strengths and weaknesses, you feed that evaluation back as refined description, giving concrete feedback and adjusted instructions, and iterate until the result meets your needs. Option A throws away a largely on-target draft and all the context built so far. Option B abandons the collaboration at the first imperfection instead of using feedback to improve it, forfeiting the efficiency the loop provides. Option D relies on random variation instead of communication, since a rerun without changed description gives the assistant no signal about what to fix. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • The Description-Discernment loop — Exercises (AI Fluency course) • The AI Fluency Index — Iteration and refinement (Anthropic Education Report) • My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
You are a student who has noticed that Anthropic's AI Fluency: Framework & Foundations course pairs two competencies: one governs how you communicate requests to an AI, the other how you evaluate what comes back.

Which statement captures the relationship the course describes?

A. Description comes first and Discernment second: you write the request, then evaluate the single result it produces.
B. Description and Discernment feed each other through a task: you describe, evaluate what comes back, and describe again.
C. Description and Discernment trade off: the more precisely you describe, the less evaluation the output needs.
D. Description hands over to Discernment with time: as the assistant learns your preferences, you describe less and review more.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B matches the course: Discernment is the flip side of Description, and the two work hand-in-hand in a continuous loop in which you describe, evaluate, refine, and repeat throughout a collaboration. Option A makes the relationship linear and one-shot, while the loop runs across every task and iteration. Option C understates the need for evaluation: better prompts improve the odds of a good result, but outputs are generated probabilistically, and the course calls critical evaluation of AI outputs a non-negotiable responsibility, so precise descriptions do not reduce the evaluation an output needs. Option D overreads what remembered preferences can do: even when an assistant's memory feature carries your preferences into new chats, each new task still has to be described, and Discernment evaluates what comes back rather than taking over from that description. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • A closer look at Discernment — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • The Description-Discernment loop — Exercises (AI Fluency course) • Use Claude's chat search and memory to build on previous context (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
You lead communications at a nonprofit. After several describe-evaluate-refine rounds, an assistant's draft of your newsletter feature meets the quality bar you set. You are deciding how to close out the task under the Description-Discernment loop from Anthropic's AI Fluency course.

According to the course, what remains before the piece is done?

A. Rerun the final prompt several times and confirm the outputs are consistent before using the draft.
B. Ask the assistant to run a final accuracy check on its own draft and confirm that it is ready to send out.
C. Add a note disclosing the assistant's role in the piece, and send the draft out in its current form.
D. Integrate your own judgment, deciding what to keep or change and taking responsibility for the final piece.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is the loop's closing step: after describing, discerning, and refining, you integrate your own expertise and perspective, make the final keep, modify, or discard decisions, and take responsibility for the output. Human judgment finishes the work. Option A misapplies a consistency check, since variation across runs is normal generation behavior, not a completion criterion. Option B hands the final check to the system whose draft is being evaluated; an assistant's check of its own work cannot replace your judgment or your accountability for the piece. Option C borrows a Diligence practice: disclosing the assistant's role is sound, but sending the draft out as it stands skips the loop's closing step, in which you make the final keep, modify, or discard decisions yourself. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) References: • The Description-Discernment loop — Exercises (AI Fluency course) • A closer look at Diligence — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You are a financial analyst about to paste a spreadsheet containing clients' names and personal financial details into a general-purpose consumer AI chatbot to speed up a report.

In the AI Fluency Framework, which Diligence component should guide this decision?

A. Creation Diligence
B. Transparency Diligence
C. Deployment Diligence
D. Product Discernment
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: Creation Diligence covers being thoughtful about which AI systems you choose and how you engage with them, including what data you share and the privacy, security, and ethical implications of doing so, which is exactly the question raised by pasting client financial details into a consumer tool. Option B concerns being open about AI's role in your finished work, a later and different question. Option C concerns verifying and taking responsibility for outputs you use or share. Option D is a Discernment skill for evaluating output quality, not a responsibility practice governing what you put in. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) References: • A closer look at Diligence — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • A closer look at Diligence — Exercises (AI Fluency course) • I would like to input sensitive data into my chats with Claude. Who can view my conversations? — Be mindful about sensitive information (Claude Help Center)

fields.Front:
You are a student finishing an essay you drafted substantially with an AI assistant and then verified line by line. Your program's academic policy expects students to be open about AI's role in submitted work, and you are deciding whether to add an acknowledgment.

In the AI Fluency Framework, which Diligence component does this decision involve?

A. Creation Diligence
B. Transparency Diligence
C. Deployment Diligence
D. Process Description
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: Transparency Diligence means being honest about AI's role in your work with everyone who needs to know, and the AI Fluency course notes that expectations differ by context; an academic program's disclosure policy is precisely such a context. Option A concerns choosing systems and deciding what to share with them, which happened earlier in the workflow. Option C, verifying and vouching for the output, is already satisfied by the line-by-line review, so disclosure is the piece still open. Option D is a Description component about guiding the AI's approach to a task, not a responsibility practice. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) References: • A closer look at Diligence — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • AI Fluency: Framework and foundations — AI diligence statement (Claude Academy) • Framework for AI Fluency, v1.1 (Dakan & Feller, Ringling College)

fields.Front:
You are a manager who receives an AI-generated competitive analysis and forwards it to the executive team 20 minutes later with a note saying it was AI-generated, but without reading it. The analysis turns out to describe an acquisition that never happened, and the executives cite it in planning.

In the AI Fluency Framework, which Diligence component would have prevented this outcome?

A. Transparency Diligence
B. Creation Diligence
C. Deployment Diligence
D. Performance Discernment
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: Deployment Diligence means taking responsibility for verifying and vouching for AI outputs before you use or share them, and reading and checking the analysis would have caught the invented acquisition before it reached the executives. Option A was actually satisfied, since the note disclosed AI's role, and disclosure alone does not make content accurate. Option B concerns the choice of AI system and what you share with it, which is not where this failure occurred. Option D evaluates the assistant's collaborative behavior during an interaction, not your obligation to verify what you pass on. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) References: • A closer look at Diligence — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Framework for AI Fluency, v1.1 (Dakan & Feller, Ringling College) • Reduce hallucinations

fields.Front:
You lead communications at a nonprofit and are adding a diligence statement to an AI-assisted annual impact report, following the model statement presented in Anthropic's AI Fluency course.

Which TWO elements does the course say the statement should include? (Select TWO.)

A. A description of how the AI contributed to the work and the review process you applied.
B. Your assertion that you remain responsible for the final content and its accuracy.
C. A disclaimer limiting your organization's liability for errors the AI system introduced.
D. Transcripts of the AI conversations that produced the report, attached as an appendix.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and B. Option A matches the course's model statement, which discloses how AI contributed to specific tasks and describes the review and evaluation those contributions underwent. Option B matches its other core element: an affirmation that you maintain full responsibility for the final content and its accuracy. Option C works against the statement's purpose, since a diligence statement affirms your own full responsibility for the work instead of limiting liability for errors the AI introduced. Option D confuses transparency with raw disclosure; the course's model statement summarizes AI's role and your review process, not verbatim transcripts. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) References: • A closer look at Diligence — Exercises (AI Fluency course) • AI Fluency: Framework and foundations — AI diligence statement (Claude Academy) • Framework for AI Fluency, v1.1 (Dakan & Feller, Ringling College)

fields.Front:
Registrations for your organization's conference workshops fell by a third this year, and you, the manager responsible, have a month to find out why with an AI assistant. Before starting, you agreed what a useful answer would look like and drew up a plan of five analysis tasks, deciding for each whether you, the assistant or both would do it. The first task, a breakdown of the registration data, is finished. It shows that registrations from returning attendees held steady and that almost the whole drop comes from first-time attendees in one region. The four tasks left in the plan (a pricing comparison, speaker ratings, a survey of returning attendees and a schedule review) do not examine that group.

What should you do with the plan?

A. Finish the four remaining tasks as planned, then examine the regional finding with whatever time is left over.
B. Revise the remaining tasks around the finding, and choose each further step from what the last one showed.
C. Give the assistant the finding and the full data set, and ask it to state the cause in a single response.
D. Set the task list aside, and redefine what a useful answer looks like before doing more of the analysis.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. Finding out why registrations fell is an open-ended investigation: which analysis is worth doing depends on what earlier analysis turns up, so the plan has to adapt as findings arrive. The first result places the drop in a group that the four remaining tasks do not examine, which makes the list as written a poor guide to the rest of the month. A list of tasks fixed up front suits work whose parts are predictable, such as preparing a workshop with known deliverables. Option A carries out that fixed list regardless and spends most of the remaining time away from the one lead the data supports. Option C asks for a conclusion that the evidence gathered so far cannot support, and a single response leaves no intermediate results to check. Option D repeats a step that does not need repeating: the goal and the definition of a useful answer are unchanged, and only the tasks that serve them need to change. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • Prompting best practices — Research and information gathering • Project planning and Delegation — Step 3: Task breakdown and delegation analysis (AI Fluency course) • Prompting best practices — Chain complex prompts

fields.Front:
A university procurement office uses Claude to review supplier contracts before signature. Policy requires the same four checks on every contract: the liability cap, the data-protection clause, the termination terms and the payment schedule. The office sends each contract with one prompt that asks for all four checks together. Reviewers find that the liability analysis is thorough, that the last two checks often receive a sentence each, and that some reviews omit the payment schedule. An engineer proposes replacing the prompt with an agent that reads each contract and decides which issues to investigate and in what order.

Which design fits this workflow best?

A. Run a fixed pipeline of four focused prompts, one per check, then a final prompt that combines the results.
B. Adopt the proposed agent, and let it choose from each contract which issues to examine and in what order.
C. Keep the single prompt, and add an instruction to give each of the four checks the same depth of analysis.
D. Run the single prompt three times per contract, and report the findings that at least two of the runs share.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The review is predictable: the same four checks are required on every contract, so the subtasks are known in advance and can be fixed as a sequence. Giving each check its own focused prompt means each one receives the model's full attention, which addresses the uneven depth and the omitted check, and a final step assembles one report. Option B suits open-ended investigations, where the next step depends on what has been found; here the steps are the same for every contract, and letting an agent choose them brings back the risk that a required check is skipped. Option C leaves all four checks competing for attention in one pass, and a general request for equal depth does not change that. Option D triples the cost while each run has the same weakness, and requiring agreement between runs drops findings that only one run caught. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • Increase output consistency — Chain prompts for complex tasks • Prompting best practices — Chain complex prompts • How the agent loop works — The loop at a glance

fields.Front:
You are a student who asks an AI assistant for feedback on an essay. Your prompt tells it to check the argument's structure against the assignment rubric first, then to comment on style, and to rewrite nothing. It follows that order and rewrites nothing, but it returns 46 comments. Most are word-choice preferences or remarks that a sentence "could be stronger." You would act on five of them: three places where the essay fails a rubric criterion and two sentences that are unclear, all scattered among the rest.

What is the most effective addition to your next prompt?

A. An instruction to be conservative and to raise the issues that it is highly confident are real problems.
B. A stricter order of work in which the whole rubric check is completed before the first style comment is made.
C. A list of the issues to report, such as failed rubric criteria, and the issues to skip, such as word choice.
D. A request for a confidence score from 1 to 10 on each comment, with the comments scored below 7 left out.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. The assistant already works in the order you asked for; what it has not been told is which issues are worth reporting, so it reports everything it notices. Naming the categories to report and the categories to skip gives it a rule that excludes preference-level remarks, and that is what raises precision. Option A sets a general bar without saying what counts as a real problem, and instructions of that kind do little to improve precision. Option B tightens a sequence that is already being followed, so the same 46 comments would arrive in the same order. Option D filters on self-reported confidence, which is poorly calibrated and measures the wrong thing: the assistant can be fully confident that a word could be stronger, and a threshold would let that comment through. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct • A closer look at Description — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You are an analyst who asks an AI assistant for a one-page memo on your company's Q3 results for the executive team, in bullet form, and the memo arrives in that form every time. The prompt ends with the sentence "Highlight the three most important risks." You run it three times on the same figures and get three different sets of risks. In two of the three memos a 1% rise in shipping costs is among the risks, and a debt ratio that is two points from breaching a loan covenant is absent.

Which revision of the prompt would most directly fix the selection of risks?

A. Describe the memo in more detail, adding the readers' roles, a word limit and a heading for each risk.
B. Tell the assistant to be careful and to highlight the risks that it is highly confident are important.
C. Run the prompt five times, and keep the three risks that appear in the largest number of the memos.
D. State what makes a risk important, such as a measure that is close to a limit in a covenant or the budget.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. The memo's form is already right; what varies is the selection, because "most important" leaves the assistant to decide afresh on each run what importance means. An explicit criterion, such as closeness to a covenant or budget limit, tells it which risks qualify, and that is what makes the choice consistent and puts the covenant ratio ahead of a routine cost change. Option A adds detail about the document, which the assistant already produces as required, and says nothing about how risks are chosen. Option B asks for care and confidence without defining importance, so the assistant goes on applying the same undefined judgment. Option C keeps whatever recurs under the vague wording, and the shipping-cost item appeared in two memos out of three, so repetition would retain it. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct • Define success criteria and build evaluations — Define your success criteria • A closer look at Description — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You run communications for a nonprofit with a distinctive voice in its social posts. Your prompt to an AI assistant includes four past posts as examples, and the drafts it writes match the voice well. For a new campaign the board has decided that posts must not name individual families the nonprofit has helped. The decision came after the four example posts were published, two of which name a family, and the prompt does not mention it. Of the last ten drafts, three name a family taken from the case notes you supplied.

Which change to the prompt most directly addresses this?

A. State the board's rule in the prompt itself, and replace the two example posts that name a family.
B. Add six more past posts to the prompt, and give the assistant a larger sample of the voice to imitate.
C. Tell the assistant to act as a communications officer who is experienced in protecting client privacy.
D. Ask the assistant to think step by step about each draft's content before it writes the final version.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. Examples steer tone and structure reliably, which is why the voice is right, but the assistant also picks up whatever else the examples show, and two of the four name a family. The board's rule appears nowhere in the prompt, so the assistant has no way to know it. Stating the rule, and replacing the examples that contradict it, removes both causes. Option B enlarges the sample of a voice that is already matched; posts written before the decision cannot demonstrate it, and those that name a family strengthen the unwanted pattern. Option C changes the persona without telling the assistant what the board decided. Option D adds reasoning time, but careful reasoning cannot apply a rule that the prompt does not contain. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.2 References: • Prompting best practices — Use examples effectively • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct • Effective prompting techniques — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You are an analyst who opens a new conversation with an AI assistant and uploads a 200-page report, which fits within the assistant's context window with room to spare. Your first message asks for every risk the report identifies. The reply lists the risks from the opening chapters and the closing chapters accurately and ends with a short summary, but it leaves out six risks that are stated plainly in chapters 9 to 12, in the middle of the report. When you ask about chapter 10 by itself, the assistant quotes its risks correctly.

Which explanation best fits this result?

A. The conversation outgrew the context window, and the earliest material was dropped or condensed to make room.
B. The reply reached its maximum output length, and the list was cut off before the remaining risks were written.
C. The upload was converted to text with gaps, and the middle chapters were missing from what the assistant read.
D. The report is a long input, and material in its middle is processed less reliably than material at either end.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. Models process the beginning and end of a long input most reliably and are more likely to miss material in the middle, and the omissions here follow position: the opening and closing chapters are covered and chapters 9 to 12 are not. Fitting inside the context window does not mean every part is recalled equally well. Asking about one section at a time, as the chapter 10 follow-up shows, or placing a summary of key findings at the start under clear section headings, reduces the effect. Option A does not fit a first reply to a report that fits with room to spare, and the earliest chapters are the ones handled well. Option B would remove the end of the list, yet the closing chapters and a final summary are present. Option C is ruled out because the assistant quotes chapter 10 correctly when asked about it alone, so the text was available to it. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.1 References: • Context windows — How the context window works • Prompting best practices — Long context prompting • Capabilities & limitations — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course)

fields.Front:
You manage a consulting team and are writing review guidance for AI-drafted client briefs. The assistant marks each factual claim in a brief as high or low confidence. Last quarter your experts checked all 1,200 claims in 60 briefs against independent sources and recorded the results by type of claim. For financial figures, dates and regulatory references alike, about 1% of the high-confidence claims were wrong and about 30% of the low-confidence claims were wrong. The experts have time to check a quarter of the claims in each new brief, low-confidence claims make up about 15% of a brief, and the assistant's underlying model is updated several times a year.

Which review policy fits this evidence?

A. Set the confidence marks aside, and have the experts check a random quarter of the claims in each new brief.
B. Send the low-confidence claims to the experts, and have them spot-check a random sample of the high-confidence claims.
C. Send the low-confidence claims to the experts, and release the high-confidence claims without a further check.
D. Have the experts check the claims in the order they appear in each brief until the time for that brief has run out.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. A model's own confidence mark is not evidence by itself, but these marks have been tested against expert-verified outcomes for each type of claim: low-confidence claims were wrong about thirty times as often as high-confidence ones. That makes the mark a sound basis for routing limited expert time. The low-confidence claims are 15% of a brief and the experts can cover 25%, so the remaining tenth pays for a random sample of high-confidence claims, which keeps measuring their error rate. That matters because last quarter's 1% describes last quarter's model, and the model is updated several times a year. Option A discards a validated signal and would reach only about a quarter of the claims most likely to be wrong. Option C leaves a tenth of the experts' time unused and stops measuring the high-confidence claims, so a rise in their error rate after an update would go unnoticed. Option D spends expert time by position in the brief rather than by risk. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • A closer look at Discernment — Key takeaways (AI Fluency course) • Define success criteria and build evaluations — Define your success criteria • Reduce hallucinations

fields.Front:
You manage a team that uses an AI assistant to draft technical white papers. A subject-matter expert has reviewed every factual claim in the last ten papers: 388 of 400 were correct, which is 97%. The expert's log shows that 11 of the 12 errors were among the 40 claims that cite clause numbers from testing standards. For future papers the expert has time to review about a fifth of the claims in each. A colleague points to the 97% figure and proposes that a meticulous copyeditor with no background in the subject take over the accuracy review.

How should the accuracy review be assigned?

A. Have the expert review one paper out of five in full, and release the other four papers after copyediting.
B. Move the accuracy review to the copyeditor as proposed, and keep the expert available for the copyeditor's queries.
C. Have the expert check the claims that cite standards clauses, and spot-check a random sample of the other claims.
D. Have the expert review a random fifth of the claims in each paper, drawn without regard to the type of claim.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. The 97% figure hides an uneven picture: 11 of the 40 standards-clause claims were wrong, more than a quarter, while 1 of the other 360 was. Reduced expert time should go where the errors are, so the expert checks the clause claims, about a tenth of the claims in a paper, and uses the remaining time on a random sample of the others to keep measuring their error rate. Option A gives one paper a full review and leaves the clause claims in the other four unchecked. Option B relies on an overall rate that masks a claim type failing far more often, and a plausible but wrong clause reference is the kind of error a reviewer without subject knowledge misses. Option D checks about a fifth of the clause claims and leaves most of the highest-risk claims unverified. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • A closer look at Discernment — Exercises (AI Fluency course) • Define success criteria and build evaluations — Common success criteria • Reduce hallucinations
